title: Afterlife Contract™
aboutParagraph: Afterlife Contract™ is a conceptual artwork disguised as a legal document. Framed as a luxury "Lifetime Lease + Eternity" agreement from Grim Reaper Inc., it puts stamps and clauses on the one thing nobody can file.
artworkCardDescription: The Underworld, curated. Cosmic symbols and old-paper texture around one final choice: three destinations, one signature, no reliable map. The soul is free; the ink is the only debt.
conceptParagraphs: Everyone gets the afterlife (or non-afterlife) for free. People would still pay for premium access, VIP status and an official confirmation.
That's the whole joke, and it's probably also true.
bureaucracyParagraph: The design borrows the visual language of law and finance—stamps, ledgers, clauses—and applies it to the ultimate unknown. Lines like "Subject to Underworld Adjustments" are there to see how far a stamp can go.
dualityParagraphs: Three options, deliberately tangled: one about fear, one about love, one about making things. Their official names stay inside the original contract.
There is no correct answer. Choosing, or refusing to choose, is the real performance.
visualLanguageParagraph: Holographic gold frames, parchment textures, cartoon skeletons, cosmic symbols and handwritten annotations. Part medieval charter, part tarot deck, part internet meme.
filedClausesIntro: Four articles explaining how free eternity acquired premium paperwork.
filedClauseSummaries: Eternity is free. The premium certificate is not.
The unknown has been issued a stamp and several unnecessary clauses.
Three destinations remain entangled until you inspect the evidence.
Part medieval charter, part tarot deck, part internet afterthought.
interactionClosing: Nobody checks which option you chose. Only you know why.
closingQuoteLines: The only thing you actually sign

downloadIntro.beforeDestinations: Feeling brave, curious, or just mildly bored with mortality? You can download a printable version of the Afterlife Contract and sign your preferred destiny—

The only "service" truly provided is a moment of reflection, a piece of digital ink paper, and the faint hope that.......
